newsitem.title: UK: British minister resigns over sleaze probe.
newsitem.headline: British minister resigns over sleaze probe.

text.p: A key minister in Prime Minister John Major's government resigned his post as Paymaster General on Wednesday after being strongly criticised by fellow members of parliament investigating allegations of so-called "sleaze".

David Willetts, one of Major's top strategists, quit after the release of a report which said he had not been "frank and open" in evidence to a parliamentary committee probing whether MPs took cash to ask questions for businessmen in parliament.

The report by the powerful Standards and Privileges Committee -- led by a senior Conservative minister -- came as close as possible to accusing Willetts of lying, which would have brought about his suspension or expulsion as an MP.

"We cannot accept much of the memorandum submitted to the committee by Mr Willetts, nor much of his oral evidence, as being accurate," said the committee, set up to halt further damage to parliament's reputation after a string of scandals.
"We are very concerned that any member should dissemble in his account to the committee and believe that this response by Mr Willetts has substantially aggravated the original offence."

His departure as Paymaster General, traditionally a Treasury post but switched to the Cabinet Office to improve the planning and presentation of government policy in the run-up to an election due by May, is a severe blow for Major.
The Conservatives technically lost their parliamentary majority last week and lagged the opposition Labour party by a huge 37 points in one recent opinion poll.

"This is another massive embarrassment for John Major, yet another example of the Government disintegrating before our eyes. This is another example of a minister whose word cannot be trusted," said Labour deputy leader John Prescott.
Scandals have now cost the jobs of nine ministers and a string of ministerial aides since Major surprised pollsters by winning the last election in 1992.

Willetts himself was tipped as a future Conservative prime minister. But critics said his reputation as an intellectual -- which won him the nickname "Two Brains" -- did not prevent his undoing through a mixture of naivety and arrogance.

Willetts' downfall came because of a memo he wrote about his conversation with the head of a committee investigating charges that another former minister took cash for questions on behalf of Mohammed Al Fayed, the owner of top store, Harrods.

The memo came to light in legal papers after former trade minister Neil Hamilton, who was forced to quit his post but maintained his innocence, dropped a libel battle against the Guardian newspaper which broke the story.
The committee's two-month inquiry into whether Willetts improperly tried to influence the probe when he was a "whip" or government business manager made front-page headlines.

The committee said Willetts should never have had the conversation with Geoffrey Johnson Smith, chairman of the members' interests committee investigating Hamilton, saying this had "gone beyond what should properly have taken place".

Willetts tried to argue that a phrase in his memo saying Johnson Smith "wants our advice" should be interpreted according to an outmoded 18th century usage meaning he merely needed some advice. His "cleverness" was widely ridiculed by the media.

Willetts said he was sorry "my integrity has been called into question, especially as throughout the committee hearing I told the truth". Major made no attempt to keep him in his post. Willetts remains a member of parliament.
"Mr Willetts is an honourable man and he had said very firmly that he believed the only course was for him to resign," an aide to Major said.
